To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the contractile performance, calcium-activated ATPase activity, and the ultrastructure of the myocardium are all altered by the development of hypertension and that these alterations are reversible by reversal of the hypertension.

reversal of hypertension results in the regression of hypertensive myocardial hypertrophy as assessed by the reversal of the contractile and biochemical changes observed in the hypertensive myocardium.

1) the contractile behavior of papillary muscle from hypertensive rats was significantly altered; 2) the biochemical alterations observed in the hypertrophied myocardium were consistent with a depression in contractile protein function; and 3) the reversal of hypertension resulted in the regression to normal of all of the contractile and biochemical alterations associated with pressure overload myocardial hypertension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of contractile and biochemical changes that occur in the heart during the development of hypertensive hypertrophic heart disease and the reversal of this process.
the study of the contractile behavior of papillary muscles isolated from the hearts of spontaneously hypertensive rats and the effect of reversal of hypertension on these parameters.
the effects of hypertension and its reversal in the rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the hypertensive heart, after 10 wk of hypertension, is characterized by an increase in heart weight, prolongations of TPT and time to half relaxation (TR50), and depression in the velocity shortening.
reversal of pressure overload hypertrophy in the rat is associated with the regression of mechanical, biochemical, and histopathological abnormalities associated with the hypertensive hypertrophy.
the reversal of pressure overload hypertrophy is a slow process that is accompanied by a gradual regression of the mechanical and biochemical abnormalities of hypertrophy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the myocardial contractile performance of the hypertrophied heart is maintained by a compensatory mechanism which is dependent on the duration and severity of the pressure overload.
the contractile abnormalities observed in the hypertensive myocardium were due, in part, to a decrease in the calcium sensitivity of the contractile proteins.
the development of hypertensive hypertrophic myocardium is associated with a depression in the velocity and extent of shortening.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reversal of hypertension can lead to the regression of mechanical, biochemical, and morphological abnormalities associated with the development of pressure overload myocardial disease.

the reversal of hypertension can lead to the reversal of hypertensive cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction, and this is a promising avenue to explore for the treatment of heart disease.
